name: Amber
lede: Amber is the warm yellow-orange of fossil tree resin, named from the Arabic and, in Greek, the origin of the word electricity, and it has been traded across the Baltic for at least thirteen thousand years.

sections.title: Two names for one resin
sections.body:
Amber is the clear yellow-brown or reddish orange of the fossil resin, and Paterson notes that the stone itself varies so much that the color word spans a wide range of shades [1]. The English word comes from the Arabic *anbar* [2]. Older lists give *karabé*, from a Persian phrase meaning attractor of straws, along with *succinum* and *electrum* [2].

The Greek name, *elektron*, is the more consequential [3]. Finlay says the Greeks linked it to the sun because the resin comes in all the colors of the sun, from bright yellow to sunset red, and because rubbed amber attracts lint and makes sparks [3]. In 1600 the English physician William Gilbert grouped amber with several other substances that attract small objects when rubbed, and named the effect electricity after the Greek word [3]. German keeps a different image: *Bernstein* means burning stone, because the nine in ten pieces below export quality were burned for their scent [3][4].

Succinite is the trade name for amber from the Baltic region [7].

sections.title: Tears of conifers
sections.body:
Amber is fossilised resin, exuded mainly by trees of the Araucariaceae and Pinaceae families, and in structure it is an amorphous polymeric glass built from terpenoids [2]. Finlay traces the Baltic deposits to conifers of vast ancient forests, and lists theories for why they wept so much resin: a warm climate, evolution, or disease [3]. He dates a piece of Baltic amber to about forty million years, and says rivers and glaciers carried some of it from the rocks to a seabed around fifteen million years ago [3]. Lumps of nine pounds or more have been found [3].

Not all amber is Baltic [6]. The amber of the Isle of Wight is 120 million years old and unrelated to the Baltic kind [6]. The idea that amber preserves dinosaur DNA, as in a famous film, is a myth for the Baltic material that dominates the trade, which is only about forty million years old [3].

The color range is wider than the word suggests. St Clair says amber runs from palest honey to smoldering ember, and can be black, red or even blue [4]. Finlay saw a collection that ran from ivory to ebony, mostly in an autumn range of yellow, orange, red and brown, with blue and black rarer, and white the most precious of all [3]. Blue amber, he says, is an ethereal ultramarine aura over something darker [3]. Finlay calls the plain resin color the one we mean by amber traffic lights [3].

Fakes abound. Real amber is old enough to be unaffected by acetone, whereas copal, which is under a million years old, and plastic will turn tacky [3]. Pressed amber is crushed powder molded under heat, with the chemistry of amber but not its history [3].

sections.title: Thirteen thousand years of Baltic gold
sections.body:
A dark red piece of amber from Gough's Cave in Cheddar, England, was found in 1950 and is perhaps the oldest traded gem-type material known [3]. A professor at Vassar College used infrared absorption in 1964 to show that it came from the Baltic and was about forty million years old, and Finlay says it was traded at least 12,500 years ago [3]. Finlay adds that the Baltic has supplied the world with amber for at least thirteen thousand years [3].

The Greeks had a myth in place of a geography [3]. Phaeton, the son of the sun god, lost control of his father's chariot and was struck down by Zeus, and his sisters, turned into poplars, wept amber into the river Eridanus [3]. Herodotus thought the story was rubbish, in part because he doubted a river that ran north into the sea [3]. Finlay notes that the real story has weeping trees, lightning, metamorphosis and a northern sea, so Herodotus dismissed it too fast [3].

About 330 BC the explorer Pytheas traveled north and, as Pliny reports, described an estuary where amber was thrown up by the waves in spring and the inhabitants burned it as fuel [3]. The Etruscans and Romans loved it, and carved pieces in the shapes of rams, monkeys or bees have been found in burial sites [4]. A Medusa head carved from a dark piece in the first century AD is now in the Getty collection [4]. One Roman historian is said to have believed that amber, which he called lyncurius, was dried lynx urine, a legend with no support [4].

In Gage's account Pliny preferred a dull yellow amber, transparent but not too fiery, and best of all one that looked like white Falernian wine, glowing gently [5]. Gage suggests this matches what Van Eyck's patrons would have known [5]. The prophet Ezekiel, Finlay observes, likened a divine fire to a brilliance like that of amber, an image that suited something the color of sunlight, exotic and from far away [3].

sections.title: Blue earth and the Amber Room
sections.body:
The greatest amber mine in the world, Finlay says, is on the Samland peninsula near Yantarny, once called Palmnicken, which now means simply Amber [3]. The amber lies in a layer of gray clay called blue earth, sitting like raisins in rye bread, and here the layer is only about 50 feet down, where in Poland and the Baltic states it is 130 feet or more [3]. Finlay found the mine in decline, with prices down, old equipment, and illegal diggers [3].

The Amber Room began in 1699, when the Prussian elector Frederick III commissioned a chamber lined with amber [3]. A Danish craftsman softened the amber into mosaics and mixed it with cognac, honey and linseed oil for color [3]. In 1716 the king's son, Frederick William I, gave the panels to Peter the Great [3]. It disappeared between August 1944, when it was crated, and April 1945, when the castle fell [3]. Finlay adds that a 2004 book claimed Red Army soldiers wrecked it, and that a replica took 25 years and $11 million to build [4].

In Gdansk, Finlay describes an icon of the Virgin given a cloak of white amber by the local artist Mariusz Drapikowski, from material donated by amber producers [3].

sections.title: Amber in the paint box
sections.body:
Amber has little to do with pigment but a lot to do with painting media. It has been used as a varnish, although it is hard to dissolve (the Pigment Compendium gives about 20 per cent solubility) [8]. Carlyle reports amber varnishes as a medium for Roberson's tube paints, while other writers warn that early authors confused amber with copal [2]. A fifteenth-century German manuscript, Clarke MS 2200, gives a recipe for a gold color that grinds amber with linseed oil and egg white [2]. Ground amber has been tentatively identified in the Palaeolithic cave paintings at Altamira, though that identification remains tentative [2].

In the eighteenth century a Parisian called Martin invented a long-lasting amber-colored varnish, whose recipe included expensive copal resin [11]. Mummy brown was mixed with a drying oil and amber varnish from the twelfth to the twentieth century [9]. In 1891 Fénéon reported that Signac used Blockx colors, ground in an amber medium [10]. In 1885 Lovibond built the first colorimeter, with a scale of browns, after realizing in Salisbury Cathedral that stained glass could serve as a standard for the amber of his beer [12]. Amber-colored glass comes from iron in the melt [17], and Ball notes iron oxide gave Egyptian glass its yellow and amber [18].

sections.title: The color of caution
sections.body: Amber is the middle light of the traffic signal in British usage, where Americans say yellow light [13]. Red, amber and green are the international standard colors of traffic light signals, as the American National Standards Institute defines them [14]. Pipes carrying other gases are marked amber, and in the alert scale Paterson describes, amber sits one step below red [13]. Photographers know it as a gel: in one of Gurney's oil sketches a head is lit by a lamp with an amber gel from one side and a blue light from the other [15]. Amber also fluoresces, giving off visible light under ultraviolet [15]. St Clair adds that the orange of the House of Orange in contemporary paintings is almost a burnt amber shade [19].

sections.title: Elixirs, lynx urine and DNA
sections.body: Amber also appears in the myth of color healing. Birren describes a color-healer named Babbitt who promoted sun-charged water under names such as cerule, rubi, amber and purpur, and quotes a case in which a patient held a vial of water near a kerosene lamp for seven minutes and drank it [16]. Birren winces at the elixirs, and the cures are a claim without evidence, as with chromotherapy generally [16]. The two myths on this page, amber as lynx urine and amber as a dinosaur DNA vault, have the same shape: a striking story attached to a real and beautiful material [4][3].

sections.title: The swatch and the stone
sections.body:
The swatch here, #FFBF00, is a saturated yellow-orange, and the ISCC-NBS block nearest it is "brilliant orange yellow", at 2.5 CIEDE2000 units [20]. Paterson describes the stone as clear yellow-brown or reddish orange, which is darker and browner than the swatch, and "amber yellow" as a rich ochre-colored yellow [1]. Our library finds amber shades recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary for the years 1423, 1500 and 1926-27 depending on the block, and RAL lists one in 1927 [20]. Other sources disagree about the shade: the 2010 XKCD color survey gives #FEB308 and #FFAD01 [20].

Hold a piece of amber to the light and then look at it by reflection. The first shows the glowing translucency that Pliny's taste praised, and the second the duller surface that screens never show [5][3]. The pairing is the quickest way to see why the swatch looks flat.

sections.title: In Japan: kihada
sections.body: Our library pairs this swatch with the Japanese yellow *kihada*, the Amur cork tree, [20]. The Pigment Compendium notes that this tree, *Phellodendron amurense*, contains high levels of berberine, a yellow dyestuff [21]. The pairing is by color and not by history: *kihada* is a dye plant and amber is a resin [20][21].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, as photographed, 28 contain this amber (within CIEDE2000 6) over at least 5 per cent of the canvas [22]. Nine of them are from India, which holds the color at ten times the expected rate, and Rajput painting alone has it in 3 of 97 works, 26 times the baseline [22]. The largest shares are a portrait of [[painting:smk-KMS1401|Tsar Mikhail Fyodorovich]], about 1650, at 56 per cent, and a Rajput page, [[painting:cma-314429|Abduction of Rukmini]], about 1640, at 46 per cent [22]. In every match the color is a highlight, meaning one of the lightest regions of its painting [22].

The 1820s are the peak decade, with 9 hits among 731 paintings, about ten times the expected rate [22]. The earliest match is a Madonna and Child with the Infant Saint John of 1510, at 13 per cent of the canvas, and no painter in the archive has it often enough to stand out [22]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [22].

In printed English the adjective amber stood at about two thirds of its 2010 peak in 2000 and rose fastest after 2000 [23]. Related colors are [[gold]], [[orange]], [[goldenrod]] and [[ochre]].

questions.q: Why did William Gilbert name electricity after amber in 1600?
choices: Rubbed amber attracts light objects and the Greek word for amber is elektron
Amber was the first stone found to conduct current
Amber was used to make batteries
questions.answer: Rubbed amber attracts light objects and the Greek word for amber is elektron

questions.q: True or false: Baltic amber, the kind that dominates the trade, is about forty million years old.
A piece sold as amber stays unaffected by nail-polish remover (acetone). What does that suggest?
choices: It is probably real, ancient amber
questions.answer: It is probably real, ancient amber

openers: Hold amber to the light: the glow Pliny praised is translucency, which a screen swatch cannot show.
Amber gave electricity its name: elektron, the Greek word for the resin, in Gilbert's 1600 coinage.
Baltic amber is about forty million years old, so the dinosaur-DNA story is a myth for most of what is traded.

issues: Finlay's dates for Baltic amber (40 Ma; 15 Ma wash-out) not cross-checked
Babbitt first name/date not given in Birren excerpt
Maerz & Paul dates for amber blocks ambiguous in library
